reasoning: Decomposed into 89 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 3 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The chief issue is an acute cutaneous eruption occurring in close temporal relationship to chemotherapy.
The patient developed the eruption 5 hours after the second romidepsin infusion.
The eruption consisted of bright, hot, salmon-pink, nonscaly, edematous nummular patches and plaques.
The eruption involved intertriginous areas, the face, the upper chest, and the back.
The patient described the skin feeling like a "heat rash."
The patient had minimal pruritus.
The skin description points to an inflammatory drug eruption rather than painful skin necrosis or severe hypersensitivity.
Strong timing with drug exposure is a salient positive finding.
The drug exposure specifically involved romidepsin infusion.
The morphology was that of well-described erythematous edematous plaques and patches.
The distribution favored body folds and intertriginous areas.
The eruption also involved the face, chest, and back.
Biopsy showed a neutrophilic infiltrate in the papillary and superficial reticular dermis.
Biopsy showed mild spongiosis.
Biopsy showed no epidermal necrosis.
The patient has Sézary syndrome.
The eruption is described as new and acute after infusion.
Progression of baseline disease is less likely.
The patient was also on bexarotene.
The immediate post-infusion onset implicates romidepsin more strongly.
There was no fever.
There was no skin pain.
There was no lymphadenopathy.
There was no mucositis.
There was no arthralgia.
There was no transaminitis.
There was no neutrophilia.
There was no eosinophilia.
Histology showed no epidermal necrosis.
These findings argue against Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.
These findings argue against DRESS.
These findings argue against classic Sweet syndrome.
These findings argue against AGEP.
Lack of mucosal involvement is especially important against SJS/TEN.
Lack of epidermal necrosis is especially important against SJS/TEN.
Lack of eosinophilia argues against DRESS.
Lack of systemic organ involvement argues against DRESS.
Lack of fever argues against classic Sweet syndrome.
Lack of neutrophilia argues against classic Sweet syndrome.
The biopsy is neutrophilic.
The leading differential is toxic erythema of chemotherapy.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy is a chemotherapy-associated eruption.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy is characterized by erythematous edematous patches and plaques.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy often involves intertriginous areas.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy can be painful or burning.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy is not necessarily severe.
Toxic erythema of chemotherapy can occur shortly after chemotherapy exposure.
Histology of toxic erythema of chemotherapy can show interface change.
Histology of toxic erythema of chemotherapy can show eccrine involvement.
Histology of toxic erythema of chemotherapy can show nonspecific inflammatory changes.
Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis lies within the toxic erythema of chemotherapy spectrum.
The patient's "heat rash" sensation fits toxic erythema of chemotherapy.
The fold-predominant distribution fits toxic erythema of chemotherapy.
The close temporal association with romidepsin fits toxic erythema of chemotherapy.
A second consideration is drug-induced Sweet syndrome.
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome is also called acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis.
Supporting features for drug-induced Sweet syndrome are abrupt onset of bright erythematous edematous plaques.
Supporting features for drug-induced Sweet syndrome include a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on biopsy.
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome fits less well because she had no fever.
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome fits less well because she had no neutrophilia.
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome fits less well because she had no arthralgia.
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome fits less well because the eruption was minimally pruritic rather than tender or painful.
The distribution in body folds favors toxic erythema of chemotherapy over Sweet syndrome.
The chemotherapy timing favors toxic erythema of chemotherapy over Sweet syndrome.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is another possibility.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is also called SDRIFE.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is also called baboon syndrome.
Flexural involvement supports symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema.
A drug trigger supports symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema.
The eruption also involved the face, upper chest, and back.
The biopsy showing a neutrophilic infiltrate is less typical for symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is usually a symmetric flexural erythema without systemic symptoms.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema remains plausible.
Symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is less convincing.
AGEP is less likely.
AGEP can occur rapidly after drug exposure.
AGEP may show neutrophilic inflammation.
The patient had no pustules.
The patient had no fever.
The patient had no neutrophilia.
Morbilliform drug eruption is also less likely.
The biopsy is neutrophilic rather than lymphocytic or eosinophilic.
The morphology is more characteristic of chemotherapy-related toxic erythema than morbilliform drug eruption.

The combination of immediate onset after romidepsin infusion, intertriginous and fold-predominant bright edematous plaques, minimal pruritus with a "heat rash" sensation, absence of systemic findings, and neutrophilic superficial dermal infiltrate without epidermal necrosis most strongly supports toxic erythema of chemotherapy induced by romidepsin.
The differential diagnosis includes toxic erythema of chemotherapy with high likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes drug-induced Sweet syndrome with medium likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes symmetric drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema with low likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis with low likelihood.
The final diagnosis is toxic erythema of chemotherapy.
